MosoFin · bank reconciliation, in plain words

Does your bank match your books?

Your books say you have one amount of cash. The bank says another. This skill proves the two differ only for reasons you can name. Whatever is left over is an error worth finding.

The 20-second version

You give it a month and the bank statement. It pulls every cash movement from your books, lines them up against the statement, explains each difference (a cheque not yet cashed, a deposit not yet landed, a fee you didn't know about), and tells you whether the two sides meet to the cent. If they don't, it shows what's unexplained. It never changes anything itself.

Why the two numbers differ

Both can be right, and still disagree

Money moves on different days in the bank than in your books. You write a cheque today; the bank sees it when it's cashed. You bank the till on Friday; the bank credits it Monday1. The bank charges a fee and pays interest without telling your books. Reconciling means walking both numbers towards each other until they meet.

The mistake it catches

"Close enough" is where errors hide

Suppose the ladders end $25.00 apart. The tempting move is to post a $25 "miscellaneous" entry so the month closes. QuickBooks itself warns against forcing an adjustment like that and says it is usually better to resolve the difference2. The skill's rule is stricter: the bridge ties to the cent, and a leftover amount is an unidentified item, not rounding.

The month closes. The duplicate stays. If that cheque is ever reissued, you pay twice.
Cheques you deposit2 daysmost become available by the second business day after deposit, under US funds-availability rules1, so a deposit still missing after weeks is not timing
Cheques you write90 daysuncashed for a quarter, the skill escalates it: it may be lost, or about to be paid twice. That age is the skill's rule, not a published standard
Then, by lawthe state'smoney nobody claims for a set period, often a year or more, becomes unclaimed property you must hand over3

The IRS expects a business to reconcile its bank account every month and to keep the deposit slips, cancelled cheques and statements that support its return4. This skill produces that reconciliation; it does not replace the records.

One honest limit

It can read your books. It cannot read your bank.

With MosoFin connected, the skill reads one side of the bridge directly: the cash balance, every payment, deposit and transfer in your books. No accounting connection shows it the bank statement. So it always asks you for the statement, and it says exactly what it did and did not conclude. Comparing the books to the books is not a reconciliation, and the skill will not call it one.

Without the statement it still does useful work: it builds the whole book side, lists the cheques and deposits that are probably still outstanding, finds duplicates and wrong-date entries, and hands you a template where the only remaining job is matching against the statement when it arrives.

How a run starts

It asks six questions before it looks at anything

  1. Use your MosoFin connection, or upload the files yourself?
    Either works. You don't need a subscription to use it.
  2. Which bank account, or accounts?
    It lists the cash accounts from your books by name. It never shows or stores a full account number.
  3. Which period?
    It never assumes a month.
  4. The bank statement, as a PDF or CSV, or at least the ending balance and the lines.
    The one thing it cannot see. It asks early so you know what the result will and won't be.
  5. When was this account last reconciled?
    Without it, an item that looks new may be months old. It will tell you the bridge starts blind.
  6. How small a difference is worth chasing?
    Your threshold decides which items get an owner and a date. The bridge still has to tie exactly.

Then it reads your answers back: "Reconciling the Operating account (…4471) for September against the statement you uploaded. Go ahead?" It waits for your yes.

What you need

Connect once, or upload two files

Connected with MosoFin

Say yes, then add the statement

  • It reads the cash balance, payments, deposits, transfers and manual entries from your books, with no exporting
  • It finds your bank accounts by name from your chart of accounts
  • You still supply the bank statement, every time
  • Helpful but optional: last month's reconciliation report
Uploading instead

Bring two files, three if you have them

  • Bank statement for the period (PDF or CSV)
  • Your books' cash activity for the same account and period: a general ledger export, plus the ending balance (a trial balance works)
  • Last reconciliation if you have one: the report, or just the date it was last done
What you get back

A bridge that balances, or the exact reason it doesn't

The two laddersBank side and book side, meeting to the cent, or not, with the unexplained amount stated plainly. It says whether a statement was supplied.
Every match, and how it was madeSame amount and date; same amount and similar wording; a cheque number or reference; or one bank line covering several entries. The weaker the method, the more you should look.
What's unmatched, sortedFees, interest, a bounced payment, a card dispute, a loan debit, or "unknown" with an owner and a date to find out.
Suggested entries, and a sign-off lineThe fee and interest entries your bookkeeper would post, each tied to the statement line that proves it. Then two named people to prepare and review, and they can't be the same person.
What it never does
  • Never changes your books. It reads and suggests. It cannot mark an item cleared or sign a reconciliation off.
  • Never calls it reconciled without the statement. A book-side total is labelled a preparation, not a reconciliation.
  • Never guesses a number. A missing item is reported as missing, with the tool or file that would have covered it.
  • Never shows a full bank account number. It's masked, always.
  • Never reads anything before you say yes.
Words you'll hear

Six terms, in plain English

Deposit in transit
Money you banked that the bank hasn't credited yet. Cash and some cheques land the next business day; most other cheques by the second1.
Outstanding cheque
A payment you wrote that nobody has cashed. Your books show it gone; the bank doesn't yet.
Bridge
The two ladders of named adjustments that bring the bank balance and the book balance to the same figure. If they don't meet, something is unexplained.
Returned item / NSF
A payment that bounced. A cheque you deposited is sent back because the writer's account couldn't cover it5; "NSF" means non-sufficient funds.
Chargeback
A customer disputes a card payment with their card issuer; the payment is reversed and the amount, plus a dispute fee, comes out of your balance6.
Preparer and reviewer
Two different people: one does the reconciliation, another checks it. Separating who authorises, who handles the money and who records it is a basic control against fraud and error7. The skill fills in neither name.
Sources

Where the facts on this page come from

Regulators, the US standard for internal control, and the software's own documentation, as published when checked on 21 October 2026. Rules and timings change, so follow the link for today's wording. What the skill does comes from the skill's own file.

  1. FDIC: Expedited Funds Availability Act (Regulation CC)Cash, electronic payments and certain cheques available next business day; other cheques generally by the second business day after deposit.
  2. Intuit: Reconcile an account in QuickBooks OnlineEnter the statement's ending balance and date, tick matching items, finish at a difference of $0.00; talk to your accountant before forcing an adjustment.
  3. NAUPA: What is unclaimed property?Uncashed cheques count; after a dormancy period with no owner contact, the holder must turn the property over to the state.
  4. IRS: Publication 583, Starting a Business and Keeping RecordsReconcile the business bank account monthly; keep deposit slips, cancelled cheques and bank statements as supporting records.
  5. CFPB: Bulletin 2022-06, Returned Deposited Item feesA returned deposited item is a deposited cheque sent back because it could not be processed against the writer's account.
  6. Stripe: DisputesA dispute (chargeback) reverses the payment; the amount and a dispute fee are debited from your balance.
  7. GAO: Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government (Green Book), GAO-25-107721, ¶10.21–10.23Segregate authority, custody and accounting; where that is not practical, design alternative controls.

Not backed by an outside authority: the 90-day and 10-business-day escalation ages, and tying to the cent rather than to a materiality threshold, are the skill's own quality rules. They are common bookkeeping practice, not a published standard.
